sentence: Shake a jar of mixed nuts, or a box of cereal, and the biggest pieces often rise to the top.
claim: When mixed grains (a cereal mix) are shaken repeatedly, the larger grains often rise to the top.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "When you repeatedly shake a box of cereal mix, the larger (and heavier) grains often rise to the top" 'Often', not always (the review also describes a reverse effect).

sentence: Scientists call it the Brazil nut effect.
claim: The effect is called the Brazil nut effect, after the seminal work of Rosato et al. (1987).
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "This phenomenon was called the 'Brazil nut effect' after the seminal work by Rosato et al."

sentence: Yet it happens even when the big pieces are heavier.
claim: The effect can happen even when the larger grains are denser than the smaller ones, so buoyancy alone does not explain it.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "One explanation is buoyancy, but the effect can happen even when the larger grains are denser than the smaller ones."

sentence: Each shake lifts the grains, and small ones tumble into the gaps under it.
claim: Percolation: during shaking, smaller grains fall into the gaps below the larger grains.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "A second contributing factor is called percolation ... Here, smaller grains fall into the gaps below the larger grains during shaking." 'Lifts the grains a little' is our plain wording of the shaking.

sentence: It can't fit down there, so it's propped up more each shake.
claim: Because the big grain cannot fall into the gaps the small ones fill, the filled gaps keep it from sinking back, so it ratchets upward.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: OPEN: Our plain wording of the percolation mechanism; the review states percolation (c4) but not this step. A person should check it against Rosato et al. 1987 (PRL 58, 1038), which describes 'the local, geometric mechanism by which the segregation is produced' (search excerpt).

sentence: Scientists have found several effects at work.
claim: Buoyancy, percolation and granular convection have each been proposed, and 'the scientific trail was mixed up again' by the reverse effect.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "However, the scientific trail was mixed up again by the discovery of the 'reverse Brazil nut effect'"

sentence: Grains can flow in a loop, up the walls and down the middle.
claim: Granular convection: shaking can make grains move upward along the walls and downward in the middle of the container.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "where the shaking leads to a flow pattern of grains moving upward along the walls and downward in the middle of the container"

sentence: And in some jars, the big ones sink instead.
claim: In a reverse Brazil nut effect, larger but lighter particles can sink in a shaken bed of smaller grains; a container shape can also be designed where the larger grains move downwards.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "Here larger but lighter particles can sink in a shaken bed of smaller grains" Picture: the sinking-ball jar is an illustration (frozen snapshot, lighter ball moved by hand), badged as such; our simulation does not reproduce the reverse effect.

sentence: Measure it: in this simulation, the big disc climbs from the bottom to near the top.
claim: In our 2D soft-disc simulation (seeded, 111 discs, floor shaken 1.0 cm at 9 Hz) the big disc's centre rises from the bottom (4 cm) to near the top of the bed.
note: OPEN: OPEN: our model, not a published measurement; a person should rerun sim.mjs and check the trace in review/. The disc fluctuates near the top rather than sitting fixed.

sentence: Unpopped popcorn kernels sink in a bowl for a related reason.
claim: There is a connection between the Brazil nut effect and popcorn, where the grains that have not popped sink to the bottom.
source_title: Mathijssen, Lisicki, Prakash et al., 'Culinary fluid mechanics and other currents in food science' (a review), arXiv:2201.12128, section 'Brazil nut effect' (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
